## Problem 0
```{r}
library (tidyverse)
library (readxl)
```

## Problem 1
```{r}
transit_sea =
  read_csv(
    "./data/NYC_Transit_Subway_Entrance_And_Exit_Data.csv",
    na = c("NA", ".", ""),
    col_types = cols(
      Route1 = "c", Route2 = "c", Route3 = "c", Route4 = "c", Route5 = "c", Route6 = "c", Route7 = "c", Route8 = "c", Route9 = "c", Route10 = "c", Route11 = "c")) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  select(
    line, station_name, station_latitude, station_longitude, route1:route11, entry, vending, entrance_type, ada) |>
  mutate(entry = case_match(entry, "YES" ~ TRUE, "NO" ~ FALSE))

dim(transit_sea)
```

The dataset contains variables including station names, locations, routes served, entrance type, vending availability, and ADA compliance. Each row represent one entrance or exit. I cleaned the data by standardizign variable names with clean_names, selecting relevant variables, reading routes variables as character, and converting entry from YES?NO to a logical variable. The dataset has `r nrow(transit_sea)` rows and `r ncol(transit_sea)` columns. The data is not tidy because the routes are spread in 11 columns rather than being in a single one. 

### Problem 1 questions
```{r}
# distinct stations
transit_sea |>
  select(station_name, line) |>
  distinct()

# ADA compliant stations
transit_sea |>
  filter(ada == TRUE) |>
  select(station_name, line) |>
  distinct()

# proportion of entrances & exist without vending w/ entry
transit_sea |>
  filter(vending == "NO") |>
  pull(entry) |>
  mean()
```

There are 465 unique stations based on station name and subway line, of which 84 are ADA compliant. Among entrances and exits without vending machines, 0.377 allow entry.

```{r}
# stations that serve the A train
transit_sea |>
  pivot_longer(
    route1:route11,
    names_to = "route_num",
    values_to = "route") |>
  filter(route == "A") |>
  select(station_name, line) |>
  distinct()

# out of those, the ADA compliant ones
transit_sea |>
  pivot_longer(
    route1:route11,
    names_to = "route_num",
    values_to = "route") |>
  filter(route == "A", ada == TRUE) |>
  select(station_name, line) |>
  distinct()
```
After restructuring the data to separate route numbers and names, I found that 60 unique stations serve the A train, 17 of which are ADA compliant.

## Problem 2
```{r}
trashwheel = "./data/202610 Trash Wheel Collection Data.xlsx"

# Mr Transh Wheel
mr_trash_df =
  read_excel(trashwheel, sheet = "Mr. Trash Wheel", range = "A2:N743") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  drop_na(dumpster) |>
  mutate(
    sports_balls = as.integer(round(sports_balls)),
    year = as.numeric(year),
    #label for this
    wheel = "mr_trash_wheel")

# Professor Trash wheel w/ dive treated as missing
prof_trash_df =
  read_excel(
    trashwheel, sheet = "Professor Trash Wheel", range = "A2:M140",
    na = c("", "NA", "dive")) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  drop_na(dumpster) |>
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(year),
    wheel = "professor_trash_wheel")

# Gwyennda
gwynnda_df =
  read_excel(trashwheel, sheet = "Gwynnda the Good Wheel of the W", range = "A2:L395") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  drop_na(dumpster) |>
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(year),
    wheel = "gwynnda")

# Stacking the datasets
trash_df =
  bind_rows(mr_trash_df, prof_trash_df, gwynnda_df) |>
  relocate(wheel)

prof_total_weight =
  trash_df |>
  filter(wheel == "professor_trash_wheel") |>
  pull(weight_tons) |>
  sum()

gwynnda_june_2022_butts =
  trash_df |>
  filter(wheel == "gwynnda", month == "June", year == 2022) |>
  pull(cigarette_butts) |>
  sum()

```
Putting the three trash wheels together gave me one dataset with `r nrow(trash_df)` observations (`r nrow(mr_trash_df)` dumpsters from mr. Trash Wheel, `r nrow(prof_trash_df)` from Professor Trash Wheel, and `r nrow(gwynnda_df)` from Gwynnda) and `r ncol(trash_df)` variables. Each row is one emptied dumpster. To keep track of which wheel collected what, I added a variable for the trash wheel name. The data set also records the dumpster number, month, year, and date, followed by the weight  and the volume. The rest of the variables count the items collected including plastic bottles, polystyrene, cigarette butts, glass bottles, plastic bags, wrappers, and sports balls. The last variable is the number of homes powered. Not every wheel tracks every item. Sports balls were only counted for Mr. Trash Wheel, and Gwynnda has no glass bottle counts, so those values are missing for the others. Across all of its dumpsters, Professor Trash Wheel collected `r prof_total_weight` tons of trash, and Gwynnda collected `r format(gwynnda_june_2022_butts, big.mark = ",")` cigarette butts in June 2022.

## Questionn 3

```{r}
# baseline data
baseline_all_df =
  read_csv("./data/MCI_baseline.csv", skip = 1, na = c("NA", ".", "")) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    sex = case_match(sex, 1 ~ "male", 0 ~ "female"),
    apoe4 = case_match(apoe4, 1 ~ "carrier", 0 ~ "non_carrier"))

#No MCI at baseline
baseline_df =
  baseline_all_df |>
  filter(is.na(age_at_onset) | age_at_onset > current_age)

# women only, saved so the paragrph below can compute the proportion of APOE4 carriers inline
women_df =
  baseline_df |>
  filter(sex == "female")
```
Both files have a line of description above the real column names, so I skipped it when importing. In the baseline data, a missing age at onset is written as a period, which means the participant stayed free of MCI during follow-up. Sex and APOE4 status were stored as 0 and 1, so I recoded them as male / female and carrier / non-carrier. To meet the study's inclusion criteria, I removed participants who already had MCI at baseline, meaning their age at onset was at or before their baseline age. `r nrow(baseline_all_df)` participants were recruited, and `r nrow(baseline_all_df) - nrow(baseline_df)` of them already had MCI at baseline, leaving `r nrow(baseline_df)`. Of these, `r nrow(drop_na(baseline_df, age_at_onset))` developed MCI during follow-up. The average baseline age is `r round(mean(baseline_df$current_age), 2)` years, and the proportion of women in the study who are APOE4 carriers is `r round(mean(women_df$apoe4 == "carrier"), 2)`.


```{r}
# Amyloid data
amyloid_df =
  read_csv("./data/mci_amyloid.csv", skip = 1, na = c("NA", "Na", ".", "")) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  rename(id = study_id) |>
  pivot_longer(
    baseline:time_8,
    names_to = "time",
    names_prefix = "time_",
    values_to = "amyloid_ratio") |>
  mutate(
    time = replace(time, time == "baseline", "0"),
    time = as.integer(time))

```
The biomarker file also has a description line to skip, and it uses "Na" as well as "NA" for missing values, so both are treated as missing. Without that, the amyloid columns would import as text. I renamed the study ID variable to `id` so it matches the baseline data, then pivoted the visits into long format so each row is one participant at one visit. The time variable is years since baseline (0, 2, 4, 6, and 8). The dataset has `r nrow(distinct(amyloid_df, id))` participants and `r nrow(amyloid_df)` rows, and some visits are missing an amyloid ratio.

```{r}

# only in the b/line
baseline_only_df =
  baseline_df |>
  filter(!(id %in% amyloid_df$id)) |>
  select(id)

# only in amyloid
amyloid_only_df =
  amyloid_df |>
  filter(!(id %in% baseline_df$id)) |>
  distinct(id)

# only amyloid and baseline removed
amyloid_removed_df =
  amyloid_only_df |>
  filter(id %in% baseline_all_df$id)
```
`r nrow(baseline_only_df)` participants appear only in the baseline data and `r nrow(amyloid_only_df)` appear only in the amyloid data. Of the amyloid-only participants, `r nrow(amyloid_removed_df)` were removed from the baseline data because they already had MCI at baseline, and the other `r nrow(amyloid_only_df) - nrow(amyloid_removed_df)` are not in the baseline file at all.
```{r}
mci_df =
  inner_join(baseline_df, amyloid_df, by = "id")

write_csv(mci_df, "./data/mci_merged.csv")

dim(mci_df)

nrow(distinct(mci_df, id))

# participants that developed MCI
mci_df |>
  distinct(id, age_at_onset) |>
  drop_na(age_at_onset) |>
  nrow()
```
After combining the two datasets and keeping only participants who appear in both, the result has 471 participants and 2355 rows (one row per participant per visit) and 8 variables. It includes each participant’s age, sex, education, APOE4 status, age at MCI onset, the visit time, and the amyloid ratio. 90 of these participants developed MCI. I exported the result as a CSV to the data directory.
